title: karma: the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita
hook: Krishna sorts workers the way a foreman might, by what drives them, and then adds a worker the strands can't hold

segments.voice: Yesterday's karma lesson was the beggar's song: not them, not the gods, not even karma. The mind turns the wheel. When something stung, what was your mind doing with it? Day one thousand two hundred six.
screen: `THE MIND TURNS THE WHEEL.` · `NOW, THE WORKER.`

segments.voice: What kind of worker are you? Not how fast, not how skilled. What's going on inside while the work gets done. Near the end of the dialogue, Krishna describes workers the way a careful foreman might, by what drives them. He reaches for the three strands from the Samkhya weeks, sattva, rajas and tamas: clear, restless, heavy. Every kind of work can be read through them, he says, and so can every worker. Then, right at the end of the list, he names one more worker, a kind the three strands can't hold.
screen: `WHAT KIND OF WORKER ARE YOU?` → `THE THREE STRANDS RETURN.` → `ONE MORE WORKER.`

segments.voice: Here's Krishna's sorting, in paraphrase. A worker free of attachment is in sattva. A worker blinded by wanting things for himself is in rajas. A worker who has lost the sense of what to do and what not to do is in tamas. And a worker who has taken refuge in him, Krishna says, is beyond the strands altogether. He reads the work itself the same way. Work offered to him, done without hunger for its fruit, is sattvic. Work done for the sake of what it will bring is rajasic. Work done to harm is tamasic. Notice what isn't on the list: any particular job. The strands don't sort cleaners from surgeons. They sort the inside. Two people can carry the same boxes up the same stairs for a friend who's moving, one for praise and one as an offering, and in these verses they are doing different work. That's the sharp edge of this chapter. On the path of action, the task is the same size for everyone. What changes is the hand behind it. And the fourth worker? Krishna doesn't describe a better technique. He describes a relationship: refuge. The worker who has handed the work over to him isn't working in sattva, rajas or tamas anymore. For devotees of Krishna, that's where the path of action is headed. For anyone else listening, the first three boxes are already a mirror.
screen: `FREE, DRIVEN, OR FOGGED.` · `WORK OFFERED, WORK FOR GAIN, WORK TO HARM.` · `THE STRANDS SORT THE WORKER, NOT THE JOB.` · `A FOURTH WORKER: BEYOND THE STRANDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch yourself work, from the inside, without working. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the next task waiting for you after this: a phone call, an email, a drive. Picture yourself starting it. Notice what's already there: an eagerness for a result, a heaviness, a calm. No grading. Then picture starting it once more, and see whether simply noticing what drives you changes anything. If you pray, you can offer that task to the One you pray to. The bell holds the time.
Karma. Work, sorted in the Uddhava Gita by the worker's inside: unattached, driven, fogged, or beyond the strands altogether. Today's word.
Your line: karma, the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita. Today, just before one ordinary task, ask yourself which worker is about to do it. Day one thousand two hundred six.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers use the three gunas to talk about the quality of everyday work and food and habits, and in the Bhagavata's eleventh book Krishna applies them to the worker and the work, with a fourth kind beyond the gunas for one who takes refuge in him.

myth: in the Uddhava Gita, some jobs are sattvic and others are tamasic
the strands sort what's driving the worker, not the job.

the one who has taken refuge in him.
work done without hunger for its fruit is called rajasic

fork.setup: two people carry the same boxes for a friend who's moving. one does it for praise; one does it as an offering, wanting nothing back. in the Uddhava Gita's terms, what's different?
options: only how fast the boxes get moved.
fork.reveal: Krishna sorts work by what drives it: done for gain it's rajasic, offered without hunger for fruit it's sattvic. same boxes, different work.

original.note: Sanskrit: beyond the gunas, the three strands; Krishna's word for the worker who has taken refuge in him.

trapdoor: what you thought: good karma means doing good jobs.
what it means: the Uddhava Gita sorts work by what drives the worker: unattached, wanting, fogged, or beyond the strands.
what a scholar hears: Bhagavata Purana 11.25, where the gunas classify knowledge, work, the worker, faith and more, with a nirguna kind for what is offered to him.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 11.25.23 (work offered to him without desire for fruit is sattvic; for results, rajasic; given to violence, tamasic)
Bhagavata Purana 11.25.26 (the worker free of attachment, blinded by desire, devoid of judgment; and the one who has taken refuge in him, beyond the gunas)
Samkhya Karika 12–13 (the three gunas, recalled from days 1172–1173)

notes: Confirm verse numbers and paraphrases: 11.25.23 (classification of work) and 11.25.26 (classification of the worker, with the nirguna worker who has taken refuge in Krishna).
11.25 also classifies knowledge, residence, faith, food and happiness by the gunas; the trapdoor says 'and more' to avoid a list that may be wrong. Confirm.
The tamasic worker is paraphrased as 'lost the sense of what to do and what not to do' (smriti-vibhrashta / devoid of discrimination); confirm the rendering.
Parallels in Bhagavad Gita 18.23–28 deliberately not cited, to keep to the Uddhava Gita.
The box-carrying example is the writer's illustration.
